title: CFOs Are Pouring Money Into AI. The Finance Function Isn't Ready For It.
content:
The numbers are in. And they are embarrassing.

Only 14% of CFOs surveyed by RGP in late 2025 said they have seen a clear, measurable impact from their AI investments. A concurrent MIT study found that 95% of enterprise AI initiatives fail outright. PwC’s 2026 global survey found that only 12% of CEOs reported AI delivering both cost and revenue benefits simultaneously. Fifty-six percent said they had seen no significant financial benefit at all.

Meanwhile, worldwide spending on AI is forecast to hit USD 2.52 trillion in 2026 a 44% increase year over year, according to Gartner. More than half of CFOs are increasing their AI budgets by over 15% this year alone, according to Bain & Company’s CFO Survey 2026.

So: money is flowing in. Value is not flowing out. And almost no one in the boardroom is willing to say why.

The reason is not the AI. The reason is what the AI is being asked to run on.

Many growing businesses are now exploring fractional cfo services in India to bridge this gap between finance capability and technology ambition, but the underlying issue runs deeper than leadership bandwidth.

The Problem Nobody Wants to Name

Here is the admission most CFOs avoid making in front of their boards:

The finance function that is being handed an AI tool was not designed to be analytical. It was designed to be a record keeper. The data it produces is inconsistent. The processes underneath it are undocumented. The chart of accounts has not been cleaned in years. The MIS is a collection of manually assembled Excel files that one person in the team understands and nobody else touches.

You cannot build a forecasting engine on that foundation. You cannot build a scenario model on that foundation. You cannot build anything on that foundation except a faster version of the problem you already have.

Bain’s research is explicit on this: AI is less effective as a standalone layer on top of legacy processes and fragmented data. To harness its full value, organizations must first modernize finance operations simplifying processes, cleaning data, and shifting to an updated architecture. The technology is not the bottleneck. The structure underneath it is.

This is the problem CFOs won’t admit because admitting it means acknowledging that the finance function the one they are responsible for is not ready for the transformation

What Is Actually Happening in Finance Functions Right Now

The CFO Alliance called 2026 “the most pivotal year the finance function has faced in a decade.” The pressure is real. Boards want AI-driven forecasts. Investors want real-time performance dashboards. Leadership wants scenario models that run in hours, not weeks.

RGP’s research found that 35% of CFOs identified data trust and reliability as their top barrier to AI ROI yet only 10% said they fully trust their enterprise data. Read that again. Nine out of ten CFOs do not fully trust the data their finance function produces. And they are investing in AI tools built on top of that same data.

The IMA found that 58% of finance professionals rate their ERP data as inconsistent making data quality the single most common readiness blocker for finance AI deployment. McKinsey’s 2025 State of AI in Finance report links readiness scores below 30 with a 70%+ AI deployment failure rate. Finance functions that score above 40 on structured readiness frameworks are 3.2 times more likely to achieve their target ROI within 12 months.

In India’s mid-market companies doing ₹25Cr to ₹250Cr in revenue the foundational problems are even more acute. Most of these businesses do not have a finance function. They have an account’s function that has been promoted to the title of finance. Statutory compliance, GST filings, invoice processing, bank reconciliations. That is the work. FP&A rolling forecasts, driver-based budgeting, scenario planning, real-time variance analysis does not exist in any structured form.

When you hand an AI forecasting tool to a team running that function, here is what happens: the tool asks for clean historical data. The team exports three years of actuals from Tally or a partially configured ERP. The data has inconsistent GL coding across periods, revenue booked across different cost centres depending on who posted the entry, and comparative periods that don’t reconcile to the audited financials. The AI tool produces a forecast. Nobody in the room trusts it. The exercise is abandoned. The subscription lapses. Another ₹8-15L written off as “tech experimentation.”

This is not a technology failure. This is a sequencing failure.

At this stage, many businesses start considering virtual cfo services in India to bring structure into planning and forecasting, but even that only works if the underlying data and processes are first fixed.

The Specific Places the Finance Function Is Broken

When AI fails in a finance context, it fails at one of three points and all three are structural, not technological.

Data architecture. The chart of accounts is the DNA of the finance function. If it is poorly structured legacy codes intact, inconsistent mapping between business units, no clear hierarchy from transaction to management report every analytical output produced on top of it is unreliable. AI does not fix a bad COA. It amplifies the inconsistency at scale. The 2025 FP&A Trends Survey found that finance professionals waste 46% of their time on data cleansing and spreadsheet updates not on analysis. That time waste is a direct symptom of structural data problems, not a workload problem.

Process rhythm. FP&A is not a tool. It is a discipline with a cadence. Rolling forecasts updated fortnightly. Variance analysis conducted mid-period, not 15 days after the period closes. Scenario models maintained as live documents, not built from scratch each quarter. Cash flow projections running 13 weeks forward on a continuous basis. Most finance teams have none of these rhythms. When AI is introduced into a function with no planning rhythm, it produces outputs with no operational context and no one knows what to do with them.

Finance-business integration. AI in FP&A only delivers value when the finance function is embedded in the business when finance understands the drivers behind the numbers, not just the numbers themselves. What is the conversion rate on the sales pipeline? What is the capacity utilisation rate in the factory? What is the customer-level gross margin? These are not accounting questions. They are business questions that finance must be equipped to ask and answer. Without that integration, an AI forecasting tool produces variance reports that finance cannot explain and the business cannot use.

This is exactly where structured support models like fractional cfo services in India start becoming relevant not as a replacement for systems, but as a way to build discipline and financial architecture.

What the Best Finance Functions Are Doing Differently

Among CFOs who have fully scaled AI not piloted it but actually deployed it in production 41% report being satisfied with outcomes, compared to 25% of those still in pilot mode. Among top-quartile AI-mature finance organisations, that satisfaction rate exceeds 60%.

The difference between the 60% and the 25% is not the tool. It is the foundation.

The leading finance organisations cited at CNBC’s 2025 CFO Council Summit are doing three things: modernising finance operations, simplifying and documenting processes, and cleaning data before deploying AI not after. Routine work is being automated on top of clean processes. Data is flowing in real time from systems that have been properly configured. Finance is becoming an insight engine because the underlying architecture was built for insight.

These organisations did not start with AI. They started with process design. Then data architecture. Then systems configuration. AI came last as the accelerant on a foundation that was already built for analytical work.

The Honest Diagnostic Every CFO Should Run

Before the next AI budget approval, three questions deserve an honest answer:

Does your finance team produce a management report that every senior leader trusts without qualification? If the answer involves the phrase “we usually adjust the numbers before sharing,” the data foundation is not AI-ready.

Can your finance team tell you today not next week what the 13-week cash position looks like? If the answer requires assembling a spreadsheet, the process rhythm is not AI-ready.

When the business makes a major decision a new product line, a pricing change, a market expansion does finance provide forward-looking analysis that shapes the decision? Or does finance confirm the decision after it has been made? If it is the latter, the finance-business integration is not AI-ready.

These are not technology questions. They are function design questions. And until the answers change, AI investment in finance will continue to produce exactly what the data shows: experiments that look promising in demos and disappear within a year.

What Needs to Change and in What Order

The sequence matters more than the ambition.

Step one is building the financial architecture: a clean chart of accounts, a consistent MIS structure, cost centre and profit centre hierarchies that match the management reporting logic, and a close process that produces reliable numbers in under five days.

Step two is establishing the FP&A rhythm: rolling forecasts, structured budgeting cycles, mid-period variance analysis, and a cash flow projection process that runs continuously, not quarterly.

Step three is finance-business partnering: embedding finance professionals in operational conversations so that the numbers being produced are grounded in business context, not just accounting entries.

Only at step four does AI become the right investment. At that point, it is not replacing a broken process. It is accelerating a designed one and the ROI becomes real, measurable, and defensible to the board.

Conclusion

The CFO who stands up and tells the board that the finance function is not AI-ready that the data is inconsistent, the processes are undocumented, and the function was built for compliance, not for insight is not delivering bad news. They are delivering the only news that will actually lead to value.

The era of buying AI for AI’s sake is over. Seismic CFO Evan Goldstein said it directly at the start of 2026: “CFOs will remain willing to invest in AI but will require clarity on how it’s tied to business outcomes.” That clarity starts with an honest assessment of what the finance function can actually support and what it needs before the next technology investment is justified.

The gap between AI ambition and AI execution in finance is not a technology gap. It is a finance architecture gap. Build the architecture first. The AI will work exactly as promised once there is something for it to run on.

Contetra builds the finance architecture that makes AI investments actually pay off chart of accounts design, FP&A process frameworks, rolling forecast models, and business partnering structures for mid-market businesses in India. This is where virtual cfo services in India go beyond reporting and start driving real financial outcomes.
